Vick faces a possible prison term of 12 to 18 months after his August guilty plea to federal conspiracy charges related to dogfighting on his property in Surry County, Virginia. The original terms of the pretrial release, set in July by U.S. Magistrate Dennis W. Dohnal, required that Vick not use narcotic drugs or other controlled substances unless prescribed by a doctor. Vick's guilty plea in the federal case came after three associates -- Purnell Peace, 35, of Virginia Beach, Virginia; Quanis Phillips, 28, of Atlanta, Georgia; and Tony Taylor, 34, of Hampton, Virginia -- admitted their roles in the operation and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors. On Tuesday, a Virginia grand jury indicted Vick and the three co-defendants on state charges of running a dogfighting ring at the home.  See a timeline of the case against Vick » . The Surry County grand jury brought two charges against Vick: one count of unlawfully torturing and killing dogs and one of promoting dogfights. Each is a felony charge that could result in a five-year prison term. Vick will be arraigned October 3 in state court in Virginia. outputs.L1:
SUSSEX, Virginia (CNN) — Suspended NFL quarterback Michael Vick must comply with stricter conditions of release after testing positive for marijuana use, a federal judge said Wednesday.

The suspended Atlanta Falcons quarterback tested positive for marijuana in a September 13 drug test, according to a court document from the Eastern District of Virginia.

As a result, U.S. District Judge Henry E. Hudson ordered Vick to “submit to any method of testing required by the pretrial services officer or the supervising officer for determining whether the defendant is using a prohibited substance.”

Those methods may include random drug testing, a remote alcohol testing system “and/or any form of prohibited substance screening or testing,” the order stated.

Vick, 27, must also participate in substance abuse therapy and mental health counseling “if deemed advisable by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer,” at his own expense, according to the order.

In addition, Vick was ordered to remain at home between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., “or as directed by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer,” the order said. He will be electronically monitored during those hours.

The conditions will remain in effect until Vick’s sentencing, which is scheduled for December 10.

“This is a very difficult time for Mr. Vick,” Billy Martin, Vick’s lead defense counsel, said in a written statement. “He will comply with the court’s new conditions regarding release.”

Vick faces a possible prison term of 12 to 18 months following his August guilty plea to federal conspiracy charges related to dogfighting on his property in Surry County, Virginia.

The original terms of his pretrial release, set in July by U.S. Magistrate Dennis W. Dohnal, required that Vick refrain from using narcotic drugs or other controlled substances unless prescribed by a doctor.

Vick’s guilty plea in the federal case came after three associates — Purnell Peace, 35, of Virginia Beach, Virginia; Quanis Phillips, 28, of Atlanta, Georgia; and Tony Taylor, 34, of Hampton, Virginia — admitted their roles in the operation and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors.

On Tuesday, a Virginia grand jury indicted Vick and the three co-defendants on state charges related to operating a dogfighting ring at the property.

The Surry County grand jury brought two charges against Vick: one count of unlawfully torturing and killing dogs and one count of promoting dogfights. Each is a felony charge carrying a possible five-year prison term.

Vick is scheduled to be arraigned October 3 in state court in Virginia. His attorneys say they are contesting the state charges on the grounds that he cannot be convicted twice for the same crime.

CNN’s Eric Fiegel contributed to this report.

Court records from the Eastern District of Virginia show that Vick, the suspended Atlanta Falcons quarterback, failed a drug test administered on September 13.
